A letter from someone they did not know (they knew Albers only through the Bauhaus): an invitation to teach at Black Mountain College for the summer. The offer: 200 dollars, room and board, round-trip train tickets for both of them, a studio each.

Failure of the first large geodesic dome (the “Supine Dome”)

Raising day: it rains. Those not involved watch from a rise under umbrellas and raincoats while the others unroll miles of colored Venetian blinds and run through the rain inserting bolts at the calculated points. The slats never stand up: the dome sags like an air bag with a little air in it. Just before, Fuller tells Elaine de Kooning it will not work but they should try anyway. Cunningham attributes the failure to a lack of means; Fuller and Penn maintain that the collapse was intended and calculated, to find the “critical point” and to show that so light a structure hurts no one when it collapses. Lippold, very excited by the tension structure, sees in it an impetus for his sculpture.

A flood of parties during the summer

Over two months, more parties than in the previous five years: small cocktail parties in the students' tiny studies, big after-dinner parties in the teachers' cottages, and a big dance at the end of the summer at which Elaine waltzes with Bucky Fuller.
De Kooning paints Asheville

During the summer, de Kooning works on his abstract breakthrough Asheville by endlessly scraping off the paint and rebuilding it — an expressionist tendency opposed to Albers's systematic experimentation.

Cage teaches in the summer session

John Cage comes as an instructor during the 1948 summer session and turns the college into a laboratory to test his emerging aesthetics, with a two-part program: rethinking the relationship between art and life, and remedying modern music's failures of communication.

At an evening of Satie recitals preceded by short talks, an angry Cage scandalizes an audience that holds Beethoven and the German harmonic tradition in high esteem (many of them former Bauhaus people), and praises Satie's emphasis on duration.

Gorky's family property, Connecticut

Gorky hangs himself with a rope prepared weeks earlier, after a colostomy (1946), his wife Mougouch's affair with Matta, poor sales, a car accident in June that forced him to wear a massive neck brace, and Mougouch's departure with their two children.
the news reaching Black Mountain

At the news, de Kooning shut himself away for days; Asheville reads in part as a tribute to Gorky (whiplash line, drips, a semilyrical evocation of nature). He is said to have told his student Pat Passlof: “Now I have a chance.”
First solo exhibition at Egan's

His first solo exhibition, dominated by black-and-white abstractions smeared with color (including Black Friday), with miscellaneous titles: Zurich, Valentine, Mailbox, Painting, Black Friday, Orestes, Light in August (after Faulkner's 1932 novel).
First solo exhibition at Charles Egan's

For his first exhibition, Bill leaves out the women and the brightly colored abstractions: he shows only black-and-white enamel paintings, all made within one year, as if in a single breath, to avoid the effect of a retrospective.
Willem de Kooning's first solo exhibition at Egan's
Nothing sells; the dealer Charlie Egan, in despair, keeps the show up through May and June, to the point of embarrassment. The only press notice: a glowing review by the young Renée Arb in Art News.
First solo exhibition
First solo show at Egan's (black-and-white abstractions); first visit to East Hampton with Kline, Pollock, Egan, and Krasner; meets the critic Thomas Hess.
First solo exhibition at the Egan Gallery
Nothing sells; the same month Elaine begins writing reviews for ARTnews (two dollars an article). They dread the summer, penniless and without prospects. MoMA will buy Painting from this exhibition.

De Kooning's first solo exhibition at Charles Egan's; a critical success. Renée Arb writes in ARTnews that his subject seems to be the crucial intensity of the creative process itself; Clement Greenberg hails “this magnificent first exhibition” in The Nation.
Willem de Kooning's first solo exhibition at the Egan gallery

No sales; the dealer Charles Egan, in despair, keeps the exhibition up through May and June, to the point that it becomes embarrassing for Bill; the press ignores it except for a short, ardently favorable review by the young critic Renée Arb in Art News.
Bill opens his first solo exhibition at the Egan gallery

Bill's first solo exhibition, prepared from fall 1946 by Elaine and Egan, who set a distant deadline; ten black-and-white paintings, no figurative work. No evening opening; Bill and Elaine do not come on opening day.

Elaine hired by ARTnews

Elaine complains to Renée Arb that the magazine's critics are graduate students who know nothing about contemporary art; Arb reports the conversation to Thomas B. Hess, who invites her to the office. She becomes an “editorial associate,” a flattering title for a freelance reviewer, and serves as an unofficial channel between downtown and the leading American art magazine, introducing Bill, Pollock, and many others to Hess.

Cage and Cunningham's first visit to Black Mountain

The college replies that it can pay nothing but offers room and board. Cunningham gives a demonstration without saying much (for him, explaining amounts to a betrayal of oneself). Cage plays sixteen sonatas and four interludes for prepared piano, the fruit of two years' work, then explains his approach at length to an intrigued but friendly community. The Alberses, back from Mexico, are present and ready to follow Cage's views all the way.
Black Mountain College, 1948 summer session

After long series of calculations (in the precomputer era), one damp morning, Venetian-blind slats are assembled as the framework of a 6.70 m (22-foot) geodesic dome. The dome does not rise and is good-humoredly nicknamed the “Supine Dome.” Fuller knew that the slats had to be doubled for strength in tension, but deliberately went ahead with insufficient material to show that one can build progressively until the structure holds.
Cage teaches at Black Mountain College and takes an interest in Artaud

During his years teaching at Black Mountain (summer 1948, then 1952-1953 depending on the sources), Cage develops a well-documented interest in the theatrical theory of Antonin Artaud, a former Surrealist, an interest he would often reaffirm later
Cage teaches at Black Mountain and develops chance

Cage's methodology of chance first emerges in the scores and events composed during his five years of teaching at the college; the seismic changes in his practice are tied to this engagement with the college.
western North Carolina

Cage stages Satie's absurdist play, performed only once until then and forgotten. Cast: the student Arthur Penn directs, Buckminster Fuller plays Baron Medusa, Elaine de Kooning his daughter Frisette, Merce Cunningham the “expensive mechanical monkey”; sets by Bill and Elaine de Kooning. Deliberately nonnaturalistic, stylized acting, with no boundary between stage space and audience. Photographed by Clemens Kalischer.

Cage stages Satie's play (1913) at Black Mountain: dialogue, deliberately humorous, winks at the audience breaking the fourth wall, pre-Marx Brothers slapstick, musical interludes, and a “Monkey's Dance” with no clear narrative connection; several faculty members play self-mocking, comic roles.
